text: The overall purpose of the light-dependent reactions is to convert light energy into chemical energy, and this chemical energy is used by the Calvin cycle to fuel the assembly of sugar molecules [ev_008].
Photosystems absorb light and use electron transport chains to convert energy into chemical energy [ev_002].
Photosystem I absorbs a second photon, resulting in the formation of NADPH, an energy carrier for the Calvin cycle reactions [ev_010].

After energy from the sun is converted into chemical energy and temporarily stored in ATP and NADPH molecules, the cell has the fuel needed to build carbohydrate molecules for long-term energy storage [ev_003].

Specifically, light-dependent reactions harness energy from the sun to produce ATP and NADPH, and these energy-carrying molecules travel into the stroma where the Calvin cycle reactions take place [ev_007].

The carriers that move energy from the light-dependent reactions to the Calvin cycle are described as "full" because they bring energy; after the energy is released, the "empty" carriers return to the light-dependent reactions to obtain more energy [ev_001][ev_005].
Light-dependent reactions store light energy in ATP and NADPH, which carry that energy into the stroma to power the Calvin cycle [ev_007].
